Consequently a scalar norm relation αα†=q forces every complex embedding of α to have modulus q^(1/2). For finite-field Frobenius π, the Weil pairing supplies precisely π†π=q; passing to the Jacobian transfers the resulting spectral circle statement to a curve.

It then uses eλ(πx,πy)=q eλ(x,y) and nondegeneracy/faithfulness on the Tate module to identify π†π with q_A, before applying the theorem to the Jacobian of C.

It then uses nondegeneracy to define the unique degree-shifted φ_* satisfying η_W(φ_*(x)·y)=η_V(x·φ^*y).

interpretation: Under the stated implication from the Hodge conjecture, the category of CM motives packages Galois action on polarized CM abelian varieties and their torsion into a motivic Taniyama extension 1→S→T→Gal(Q̄/Q)→1 with a finite-adelic section. Langlands's conjugation cocycle separately twists Shimura data and produces a conjectural Taniyama group. Deligne identifies the two constructions through the specific characterizing property that their actions on CM abelian varieties and torsion are compatible with the Shimura–Taniyama results. A separate geometric embedding into a larger Shimura variety rich in type-A1 subvarieties supplies the indirect route to the conjugation conjecture.

It records Langlands's one-cocycle and Deligne's recognition of the associated conjectural group, then says their Shimura–Taniyama-consistent actions characterize and identify the groups. It also records Piatetski-Shapiro's embedding proposal, the failed direct attempt, the author's proof of the conjugation conjecture, and Shimura's conjecture as a consequence.

The gain is an object-level criterion for identifying the motivic and cocycle constructions in this CM setting; the loss is dependence on the stated Hodge-conjecture implication and on characterization results not proved in the span. The larger-variety embedding is a distinct bridge: it changes the geometric setting to make the conjugation problem tractable, without furnishing a direct proof of Shimura's conjecture.
